items.headline: Iran's IRGC declares the Strait of Hormuz 'closed' after two supertankers strike mines and catch fire
items.summary: Early Saturday Oct 17, two VLCC-class supertankers each carrying 2M+ barrels of crude struck naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz and caught fire/exploded; the IRGC Navy then declared the Strait "closed" and warned that passage of vessels of all nationalities is prohibited, with at least five tankers reported hit since Friday (one by an RPG from a small boat, per UKMTO). Brent had already settled near $109.86 Friday (+3.7%) and WTI above $101 on the week's earlier attacks, with Gulf transit volumes down to ~68% of the pre-crisis 17.1M bpd baseline.
items.actionable: This is a material escalation beyond Friday's risk premium (an actual declared closure, not just elevated odds) that should be the first thing checked at Monday's open -- it strengthens the safe-haven case for the gold/silver sleeve and raises tail risk for any new equity add from the cash pile until shipping-insurance and flow data confirm whether transit has genuinely stopped.

items.headline: CoreWeave contagion spreads from one company to the whole AI-datacenter junk bond market
items.summary: A Bloomberg report published Oct 17 says CoreWeave's bond rout is now 'shutting down' the broader AI junk-credit market, as buyers of high-yield debt increasingly freeze out other AI/datacenter borrowers seeking financing, not just CoreWeave itself. CoreWeave's own 2030 bonds were yielding above 15% this week and its 5-year CDS had priced in a >60% five-year default probability, and the stock fell toward a cumulative ~42% slide from its recent high.
items.actionable: The move from a single-name credit scare to a market-wide AI-financing freeze is the more important read-through than Friday's headline Nasdaq drop -- it argues for staying underweight HK/US tech-adjacent exposure into next week and treating any further yield/dollar decline from this stress as an additional (if fragile) tailwind for the silver/miner sleeve.

items.headline: September CPI runs hotter than forecast: headline 3.7% y/y, core 2.6% y/y
items.summary: The actual September 2026 CPI print (released Oct 14) came in above consensus: headline CPI rose to 3.7% y/y (vs. 3.6% forecast, 3.4% prior) and core CPI rose to 2.6% y/y (vs. 2.5% forecast, 2.4% prior, a five-year low in August). This resolves the forecast-vs-previous gap flagged by this week's calendar and confirms inflation re-accelerated rather than cooling further.
items.actionable: A hotter-than-forecast CPI print is the inflation backdrop the Oct 27-28 FOMC must weigh against Warsh's dovish-sounding silence -- it is a modest medium-term support for gold/silver as an inflation hedge but raises the odds of hawkish post-meeting language that could pressure the SGX bank/REIT sleeve's rate-sensitive names.

items.headline: PPI and retail sales both smash forecasts, muddying the Fed's inflation-vs-growth read
items.summary: September PPI rose 1.3% m/m (vs. 0.5% forecast, 0.4% prior) and 6.3% y/y, while headline retail sales rose 0.8% m/m (vs. 0.3% forecast) -- though gasoline drove most of the retail beat, with sales ex-vehicles-and-gas up just 0.2%. The combination of hot producer prices and resilient (if gasoline-skewed) consumer spending is a stagflation-tilted print that complicates any clean Fed narrative heading into the Oct 27-28 decision.
items.actionable: Hot PPI plus gasoline-driven retail sales (with oil now spiking further on the Hormuz closure) is a combination that keeps upside inflation risk alive even as growth looks fine -- a reason to treat the SGX bank/REIT sleeve's rate-cut hopes skeptically and to lean on the structural silver deficit rather than a dovish Fed as the thesis for the miners.

items.headline: Fed's Warsh stays silent on rate signal in Bangkok, but market reads it as dovish -- Oct hike odds fall from ~27% to <15%
items.summary: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh declined to preview the Oct 27-28 FOMC decision, reiterated a commitment to price stability, and warned AI capex could deliver a 'bumpy,' inflationary shock to the economy while noting 'no free riders' in a synchronous global central-bank tightening cycle. Despite the hawkish-sounding inflation warnings, markets interpreted his refusal to signal a hike as dovish, pushing the priced probability of an October hike down from roughly 27% pre-speech to under 15% after.
items.actionable: A hold is now the heavily consensus base case for Oct 28, which is constructive for the gold/silver sleeve and the SGX bank/REIT names, but the gap between Warsh's hawkish inflation rhetoric and the market's dovish read of his silence is a setup for a volatile post-meeting reaction if the actual statement leans hawkish.

items.headline: Gold/silver rally remains a Treasury/credit-driven safe-haven bid, now reinforced by the Hormuz closure
items.summary: The 10-year Treasury yield fell to roughly 5.09% and the dollar weakened Friday as investors rotated into bullion on CoreWeave-driven debt-financing worries; gold rose to $4,186.70 and silver to $57.13, with GDX outperforming spot silver on miners' operating leverage. Saturday's Strait of Hormuz closure adds a second, independent safe-haven driver on top of the AI-credit scare heading into Monday.
items.actionable: With both an AI-credit event and a live Hormuz closure now driving the safe-haven bid simultaneously, the setup into Monday is unusually supportive for the silver/miner sleeve, though a clean, hawkish-leaning Oct 27-28 FOMC hold remains the key risk that could unwind the yield/dollar leg of the rally even if the geopolitical leg persists.

items.headline: Silver Institute: 2026 marks a sixth straight annual global supply deficit
items.summary: The Silver Institute confirms 2026 will be the sixth consecutive year silver demand exceeds mine and recycling supply, with roughly 762M oz drawn from above-ground reserves since 2021; estimates of the 2026 gap range from ~46M to ~67M oz. Mine supply is structurally rigid because most silver is produced as a byproduct of gold, copper and zinc mining, meaning the deficit cannot close quickly even as prices rise.
items.actionable: The structural deficit is the multi-year fundamental case underpinning the book's silver/miner overweight independent of this week's news flow -- any near-term pullback on a hawkish Fed surprise is a dip to add from cash rather than a thesis change.

items.headline: Correction: the China rare-earth truce deadline is Jan 10, 2027, not Nov 10, 2026 -- already extended since the Sept 23 Trump-Xi summit
items.summary: Coverage this weekend clarifies that the broader US-China trade truce covering rare-earth export licensing (announced by Treasury Secretary Bessent on Sept 23 as Xi arrived for his state visit) was already extended two months, from Nov 10, 2026 to Jan 10, 2027 -- superseding the Nov 10 expiry some outlets (including this file previously) were still citing as the live deadline. The White House maintains China's actual rare-earth shipments and promised farm purchases remain below agreed levels despite the truce being in force.
items.actionable: The real binary catalyst for the rare-earth basket is now Jan 10, 2027, not Nov 10 -- this pushes out urgency on the Western-supply-chain trade by two months, but the White House's own complaint that shipments are lagging the truce's terms keeps a reinstatement/tightening risk alive even before that date.

items.headline: MP Materials slips to $41.71 (-2%) as rare-earth sector remains 48-75% off 52-week highs despite pending Dy/Tb ramp
items.summary: MP Materials traded between $39.88 and $42.52 Saturday, closing down roughly 2% to $41.71 and down about 16% year-to-date, with sentiment weighed down by questions over milestone-linked government reimbursements. The company remains on track to begin commissioning heavy rare-earth separation (dysprosium/terbium) capacity at Mountain Pass later in 2026, a catalyst that has not yet arrived even as four major rare-earth equities sit 48-75% below their 52-week highs.
items.actionable: The sector-wide drawdown looks more like a 'buy the rumor, sell the wait' liquidity problem than a thesis break, given the pending Dy/Tb production milestone and the now-later Jan 10, 2027 truce deadline -- this argues for patience on the rare-earth basket rather than adding into continued weakness before a concrete production or policy catalyst lands.

items.headline: China's CXMT DRAM breakthrough keeps extending the memory-chip rout into a second week
items.summary: CXMT's Oct 13 claim of a 4F-square/VSG DRAM architecture rivaling Samsung and SK Hynix continues to weigh on Korean and Taiwanese chipmakers, with the selloff bleeding into HK-listed SMIC via sympathy and compounding the CoreWeave-driven Nasdaq slide. Micron, Samsung and SK Hynix remain the epicenter of the longest chipmaker losing streak since 2008.
items.actionable: The CXMT overhang is structural (a genuine competitive threat), not a one-day scare, so any Monday HK-tech bounce should be treated as tradeable relief rather than a signal to add from the cash pile.

items.headline: Crypto ETFs bleed $610.7M over the week as Ethereum outflows overtake Bitcoin's amid hot-inflation risk-off
items.summary: US spot crypto ETFs saw a combined $610.7M in net outflows Oct 12-16, split $320.1M from Ethereum funds (93.4% via BlackRock's ETHA) and $228.4M from Bitcoin funds, as hotter-than-expected US inflation data strengthened higher-for-longer rate expectations and drove broader risk-off. Bitcoin was roughly flat into the weekend near $81,600-81,650, while Ethereum has fallen about 10.2% since Oct 1 to roughly $2,420-2,430.
items.actionable: Both legs of crypto are now seeing institutional outflows rather than just ETH underperforming BTC as in Friday's daily snapshot -- this is a weekly confirmation that the AI-credit and hot-inflation risk-off is denting even the most liquid 24/7 risk asset, reinforcing caution on redeploying cash into anything high-beta before Monday's equity open clarifies.

items.headline: STI closes +0.25% at 5,417.07 as DBS/OCBC/UOB stabilize after the Oct 6-9 yield-driven selloff
items.summary: The Straits Times Index rose 0.25% to 5,417.07 on Friday with positive breadth (127 advancers vs 49 decliners), as DBS, OCBC and UOB traded firmer following their early-October slide tied to the US 10-year yield spike to 5.32%. Friday's STI close predates the evening CoreWeave/Nasdaq rout, Friday's renewed 10-year yield decline to ~5.09%, and Saturday's Hormuz closure, all of which are relevant for Monday's open.
items.actionable: SGX banks' stabilization is constructive for the book's bank sleeve, but Monday's open will need to digest both the US AI-credit contagion and the Hormuz-driven oil spike/closure, both of which argue for watching the open rather than adding to banks/REITs pre-market.
